topics.title: Engineering vs coding
topics.technical: Software engineering is building software that survives change, scale and teams — not just making it run once. Requirements, design, testing, maintenance and communication surround the code, and most cost lives after the first release.
topics.simple: Writing code that a team can keep running and changing for years, not just today.

topics.title: The software development lifecycle
topics.technical: From requirements through design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance, the SDLC frames the work; Agile iterates it in short loops with feedback, replacing big-bang plans that meet reality too late.
topics.simple: The full journey of software — and why building it in small, feedback-driven loops beats one giant plan.

topics.title: Version control and collaboration
topics.technical: Git tracks history and enables parallel work through branches and pull requests; trunk-based or feature-branch flows structure teams. Clean history and reviewed changes are how many people edit one codebase without chaos.
topics.simple: How a whole team edits the same code without overwriting each other.

topics.title: Requirements and specifications
topics.technical: Vague requirements produce wrong software efficiently. User stories, acceptance criteria and edge cases turn wishes into buildable, testable statements — clarifying before coding is the cheapest fix there is.
topics.simple: Pinning down exactly what to build before building the wrong thing well.

topics.title: Data structures
topics.technical: Arrays, lists, stacks, queues, hash maps and trees each trade time against space for particular operations; choosing the right one is often the difference between fast and unusable. This is the shared vocabulary of the field.
topics.simple: The containers that hold data — each fast at different jobs, and choosing well is half of performance.

topics.title: Algorithms and complexity
topics.technical: Big-O describes how work grows with input; sorting, searching and graph traversal are the recurring patterns. You rarely invent algorithms, but you constantly choose and combine them — and recognise the O(n^2) that will not scale.
topics.simple: How to tell fast code from code that dies as data grows.

topics.title: Object-oriented design
topics.technical: Classes bundle state and behaviour; encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism organise larger systems. Modelling the domain in objects — and hiding what callers should not touch — keeps growth manageable.
topics.simple: Organising code into things that own their data and behaviour, so systems can grow.

topics.title: SOLID and design principles
topics.technical: SOLID — single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion — plus DRY and YAGNI guide code toward change-tolerance. They are heuristics, not laws, but ignoring them compounds interest.
topics.simple: A handful of guidelines that keep code flexible instead of brittle as it grows.

topics.title: Design patterns
topics.technical: Patterns name recurring solutions — factory, strategy, observer, adapter — giving teams shared vocabulary. The skill is recognising when a pattern fits, and resisting forcing one where plain code would do.
topics.simple: Named, reusable solutions to problems that keep coming up — used sparingly.

topics.title: Clean code
topics.technical: Readable names, small functions, honest comments and low nesting make code a team can change. Code is read far more than written; optimising for the reader is optimising for cost.
topics.simple: Writing code the next person — often you — can understand and safely change.

topics.title: Testing strategy
topics.technical: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests form a pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer slow broad ones. Tests document behaviour and let you refactor without fear; TDD writes them first.
topics.simple: A layered safety net that lets you change code without breaking it silently.

topics.title: Debugging systematically
topics.technical: Debugging is science: reproduce, hypothesise, isolate with a bisection, fix the cause not the symptom, and add a test so it never returns. Guessing scales worse than the bug.
topics.simple: Finding the real cause of a bug by narrowing it down, not by guessing.

topics.title: Databases and data modelling
topics.technical: Relational schemas, normalisation, keys and indexes shape how data is stored and queried; the model outlives the code on top of it. A wrong data model taxes every feature forever.
topics.simple: Designing how data is stored so every future feature stays easy.

topics.title: APIs and interfaces
topics.technical: Well-designed interfaces hide implementation and stay stable while insides change; REST, versioning and clear contracts let components and teams evolve independently. The boundary is the product.
topics.simple: The agreed-upon boundaries that let parts of a system change without breaking each other.

topics.title: Concurrency and performance
topics.technical: Parallelism speeds work but invites races and deadlocks; measure before optimising, because intuition about bottlenecks is usually wrong. Correct-then-fast beats fast-then-debugged.
topics.simple: Doing many things at once safely — and speeding up only what measurement proves is slow.

topics.title: System design fundamentals
topics.technical: Larger systems balance load balancers, caches, queues, databases and services against scale, latency and failure. Trade-offs — consistency vs availability, cost vs speed — are the substance of senior work.
topics.simple: How the big pieces fit so a system stays fast and up as users multiply.

topics.title: Architecture patterns
topics.technical: Monolith, microservices and event-driven designs each suit different scales and teams; premature microservices are a common self-inflicted wound. Architecture follows the organisation and the load, not fashion.
topics.simple: The overall shapes systems take — and choosing one for real reasons, not hype.

topics.title: CI/CD and delivery
topics.technical: Automated build, test and deploy pipelines ship changes safely and often; small frequent releases lower risk versus rare big ones. Delivery is an engineering capability, not an afterthought.
topics.simple: Automating the path from commit to production so releases are boring and frequent.

topics.title: Documentation and communication
topics.technical: Code says how; docs and design records say why. READMEs, architecture notes and decision logs carry the context that keeps a codebase understandable as people come and go.
topics.simple: Writing down the why, so the next engineer inherits understanding, not a mystery.

topics.title: Working on a team
topics.technical: Estimation, code review, standups and handling disagreement are the human protocols of shipping software. Most projects fail on coordination, not on code — these skills are load-bearing.
topics.simple: The human side of shipping — reviews, estimates, and disagreeing well.

topics.title: The capstone
topics.technical: Design and build a non-trivial application with clean architecture, tests, CI, documentation and a git history a reviewer can read. It demonstrates engineering judgment, not just working code.
topics.simple: One well-built, well-documented project that shows you engineer, not just code.
